name: Katarmal Sun Temple
description: A 9th-century Surya temple built by Katyuri king Katarmalla, oriented to catch the first rays of the rising sun. The main shrine sits ringed by 45 smaller stone temples on a 2,116m ridge. The original carved wooden doors were stolen and what remains was relocated to the National Museum in Delhi after a 10th-century idol theft — but the stone work and the sunrise alignment are still on site.
why_hidden: Most Almora visitors stop at Kasar Devi or push to Jageshwar; Katarmal sits 19km out on a side road with a 1.5km uphill path and zero shops, so coach groups skip it.
best_time: Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov; clear pre-noon light is best for photos
how_to_reach: 19km north of Almora on the road toward Kosi; park at Adhauli village and walk 1.5km up a stone path. ASI signage at the trailhead.
tips: ASI-managed, no entry fee. Wear grippy shoes — the stone path is polished smooth. Allow 1.5-2 hours including the climb. No toilets or food at the temple; carry water.

name: Vasudhara Falls (Mana)
description: A 120m waterfall above Mana village, the last Indian settlement before Tibet. The trek climbs from Mana past the Saraswati temple — one of the few places the Saraswati surfaces above ground before joining the Alaknanda. Local belief says the water of Vasudhara avoids those who haven't earned it; you'll see it shift in the wind from a distance.
why_hidden: Badrinath day-trippers stop at Bheem Pul and Vyas Gufa in Mana but turn back before the 6km climb to the falls.
best_time: May-Jun and Sep-Oct (only when Badrinath temple is open); avoid monsoon for landslide risk on the trail
how_to_reach: Drive 4km from Badrinath to Mana village. Trek 6km one-way from the Saraswati river bridge — 2 hours up, 1.5 down. Trail is rocky, gradual ascent to ~3,800m.
tips: Carry water and a windcheater — the spray gusts unpredictably. Start by 7am; afternoons cloud over fast. No food beyond Mana village; pack snacks. Altitude can hit hard, walk slow.

name: Sattal Birding Trails
description: A linked group of seven freshwater lakes 8km from Bhimtal that draws serious bird photographers from October to June — around 400 species recorded across Sattal, Naukuchiatal and Bhimtal. The forest tracks above Studio Lake hold thrushes, woodpeckers, the rufous-bellied niltava, and laughingthrushes that come to feed at known photography hides.
why_hidden: Bhimtal day-trippers stop at the lake island aquarium and head back; the birding tracks start a kilometre off the road and need a guide or eBird hotspot map to navigate.
best_time: Oct-Jun for birds; Dec-Jan peak activity, Apr-May for breeding plumage
how_to_reach: 8km from Bhimtal toward Bhowali; Studio Lake and Mehragaon side trails branch off the main Sattal road. Local guides at the Sattal Christian Ashram or via Sattalbirding.com.
tips: Pre-book a local guide (~Rs 1500-2500/day) for hide access — Prabhu's Hide is the best-known. Carry a 400mm+ lens; mornings are best. Wear muted colours, no perfume.

name: Pariyadeva Pashan
description: A megalithic stone alignment from roughly 1500-500 BCE on the Almora-Binsar road — long stones carved with cup-marks that nobody has fully deciphered. On the winter solstice the rising sun aligns with one of the stones. Plus you get the same uninterrupted Nanda Devi-Trisul-Panchachuli line you came to Binsar for, with maybe two other people there.
why_hidden: Most Binsar visitors only do Zero Point and the KMVN; Pariyadeva sits 7-8km off the sanctuary road with no signage in English and no entry kiosk.
best_time: Oct-Mar for clear skies; the winter solstice (Dec 21-22) is the alignment day
how_to_reach: On the Almora-Binsar road, ~33km from Almora town and 8km before the Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary gate. Ask locally for 'Pariyadeva' — Google Maps pin is approximate.
tips: No fee, no facilities — bring water and a hat. Pre-dawn arrival for the sunrise alignment in winter; the stones are spread across a ridge, so allow an hour to walk between them.

name: Tiger Falls
description: One of Uttarakhand's highest direct-drop waterfalls — about 95m of single-shot fall through deodar forest. The trek down from Chakrata cantonment passes terraced fields and a couple of Jaunsari hamlets before the final descent to a natural pool at the base where you can swim if it's not in spate.
why_hidden: Chakrata is a partial-cantonment town that doesn't appear on most Uttarakhand circuits; Tiger Falls is 5km below the road with no organised tour ops.
best_time: Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov; full force just after monsoon (Sep-Oct), reduced flow Apr-May. Avoid Jul-Aug for slippery descent.
how_to_reach: From Chakrata taxi stand, drive 12-15km to the Tiger Falls trailhead near Lakhwar. 5km downhill trek (1.5-2 hours down, 2-2.5 hours up). Last 1km is steep stone steps.
tips: Trekking shoes mandatory — the stone path is slick. Carry water and snacks; one chai stall at the trailhead is unreliable. Don't attempt in heavy rain. Foreign nationals need permits for some Chakrata side-roads, check at Chakrata SDM office.

name: Mayawati Advaita Ashrama
description: Founded in 1899 at Vivekananda's instruction by his English disciples James and Charlotte Sevier, on a tea estate at 1,940m above Lohaghat. Vivekananda himself visited in January 1901. As an Advaita Vedanta study centre, no idols are worshipped — not even Ramakrishna's — which makes it unlike anything else in the Kumaon temple circuit. The 1898 library and the museum hold his original correspondence.
why_hidden: Champawat itself sees almost no through-traffic; the ashram is another 22km up a side road from Champawat town, 9km past Lohaghat.
best_time: Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov. Closed to visitors during select retreat periods — call ahead.
how_to_reach: 22km from Champawat / 9km from Lohaghat on the road toward Pithoragarh. Last 3km is a quiet tea-estate lane. Buses to Lohaghat then shared taxi.
tips: Silence expected on the grounds. No photography inside the shrine or library. Free entry, modest dress required. Day visitors only unless on a pre-approved retreat. The ashram runs the publishing house behind 'The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda'.

name: Patal Bhuvaneshwar Cave Temple
description: A limestone cave temple about 38km from Chaukori — 90 feet underground, 160m deep — where stalactites and stalagmites have been read for centuries as Hindu deities. The Skanda Purana mentions it as the abode of 33 crore gods. You crawl down a narrow stone passage into a cathedral-sized inner chamber; a temple priest (Bhandari family, hereditary custodians) walks you through which formation is which.
why_hidden: The cave can only take small groups at a time, the priests don't market it, and it's two hours of mountain road from the nearest hotel cluster.
best_time: Year-round; cave is climate-stable. Avoid heavy monsoon (Jul-Aug) for road conditions.
how_to_reach: Drive 38km from Chaukori via Berinag and Gangolihat (2-2.5 hours). Pay entry at the cave office; priest guides you. Total time inside ~45 mins.
tips: Small entry fee (Rs 100-200 last reported). No photography permitted inside the cave. Wear shoes with grip — the descent is steep stone steps. Not suitable for severe claustrophobia or mobility issues; some sections require crawling. Carry a torch even though there's lighting.

name: Deoria Tal
description: A small longitudinal lake at 2,438m hidden inside the forest above Sari village. Chaukhamba and the Mandakini range mirror perfectly on the surface in the still pre-dawn — the reflection that gets posted as 'Tungnath' on Instagram is almost always actually shot here. The lake is mentioned in the Mahabharata as the spot where the Yaksha tested Yudhishthira.
why_hidden: The Tungnath–Chandrashila trekkers focus on the temple and summit, skipping the 2.5km uphill from Sari; Chopta day-visitors don't drive the extra 14km to the trailhead.
best_time: Apr-Jun and Sep-Nov for clearest reflections. Pre-dawn is non-negotiable for the mountain mirror.
how_to_reach: Drive 14km from Chopta to Sari village. 2.5km uphill trek (1-1.5 hours) on a well-marked stone path through oak and rhododendron. Camp permitted near the lake (forest department fee).
tips: Reach the lake by 5:30am for sunrise — by 8am the wind ripples the surface. Camping costs ~Rs 200 per tent at the forest hut; water available. Carry a torch for the pre-dawn climb. Sari has a few homestays for early-night sleep before the climb.

name: Sitabani Buffer Zone
description: A reserve forest in the Corbett landscape with an 18th-century temple at its core, dedicated to Sita — local belief is she spent part of her exile here with Luv and Kush. Unlike Dhikala or Bijrani, Sitabani sits outside the core zone: no tiger guarantee, but also no permit lottery, leopards and elephants regular, and the forest stays open through monsoon when the core zones close.
why_hidden: Tour operators push the core-zone safaris; Sitabani has no hotel cluster and the buffer-zone safari isn't ticked off any standard 'Corbett' itinerary.
best_time: Open year-round — uniquely useful Jul-Sep when core zones close. Nov-Feb best for bird density.
how_to_reach: 25km from Ramnagar via Teda Gate. Jeep safaris bookable on-site at the forest office or in advance via the Uttarakhand forest portal. No core permit needed.
tips: Half-day safari ~Rs 3500-5000 per jeep (6 pax). Carry binoculars for birds — sightings of crested serpent eagles and great hornbills are regular. The temple is a separate stop, ASI-protected. Entry fee modest. Don't expect tiger sightings — go for the forest.

name: Surkanda Devi Temple
description: One of the 51 Shakti Peethas — Hindu mythology places the head of Sati here when Shiva carried her body across the subcontinent. The temple sits at 2,750m on a peak above Kaddukhal village; a clear morning gives 360 degrees of Bandarpunch, Swargarohini, Chaukhamba and (on rare days) Nanda Devi. A short ropeway now runs alongside the 1.5km trail for those who can't climb.
why_hidden: Dhanaulti's main draws are the Eco Park and Camp Thangdhar; Surkanda is 9km away with a steep approach that filters out casual visitors.
best_time: Apr-Jun and Sep-Nov; clearest views in Oct-Nov. Snow possible Dec-Feb. Ganga Dussehra mela in May-Jun draws crowds.
how_to_reach: 9km from Dhanaulti / 35km from Mussoorie via Kaddukhal village. From Kaddukhal, 1.5km steep trek (45 mins) or the 502m ropeway (10-15 mins).
tips: Ropeway tickets ~Rs 175-200 round-trip; runs roughly 8am-5pm. Trek path has stalls for tea and prashad. Closed-toe shoes — the stone is uneven. Stash heavy bags at Kaddukhal parking. Avoid mid-day Sundays and during Navratri for crowds.

name: Gopinath Temple
description: An ancient stone temple in the heart of Gopeshwar town, the official winter abode of Lord Rudranath — when Panch Kedar's third temple closes by November snowfall, the deity is carried down here for six months of worship. The temple itself predates most of the Garhwal pilgrimage circuit; the iron trishul outside the sanctum is rumoured to never rust despite open exposure for centuries.
why_hidden: Gopeshwar is mostly known as the Chamoli district HQ and a transit stop on the Joshimath road; few pilgrims realise this is where Rudranath actually lives in winter.
best_time: Year-round; Nov-Apr is when the deity is in residence (the only time you can have darshan of the Rudranath idol without the 22km trek).
how_to_reach: Within Gopeshwar town, walking distance from the bus stand. The temple is open dawn to dusk with a midday closure.
tips: Free entry. Check the iron trishul behind the temple — locals say the lack of rust is the proof. Modest dress, leather items off before entering. If on a Panch Kedar circuit, time your visit between Nov and Apr for the winter abode darshan.

name: Triyuginarayan Temple
description: A small Vishnu temple in a village above Sonprayag where local tradition places the wedding of Shiva and Parvati. An 'akhand dhuni' — a fire pit in front of the temple — has been kept burning continuously for what locals say is three yugas (the temple's name). Couples now circle this fire for their pheras; it's quietly become Garhwal's wedding spot, but for a 5am visit you'll often have it to yourself.
why_hidden: Most Char Dham yatris pass through Guptkashi on the Kedarnath route and never make the 25km detour to a temple their travel agent didn't list.
best_time: Apr-Jun and Sep-Nov. Closed access during heavy monsoon. May-Jun is peak wedding season — go off-shoulder for solitude.
how_to_reach: 25km from Guptkashi via Sonprayag. Last 5km is a steep climb to Triyuginarayan village; cars manage but slowly. Buses irregular — taxi from Guptkashi (~Rs 1500-2000 round-trip).
tips: Free entry. The akhand dhuni is in the courtyard — you can collect ash as prashad. If interested in the wedding ritual, the temple committee runs a basic booking system at modest cost. Combine with Gauri Kund (where Parvati is said to have done penance) on the Kedarnath road, 5km away.

name: Daksha Mahadev Temple, Kankhal
description: The temple at Kankhal marks the site where Sati immolated herself in her father Daksha's yagna fire after he insulted Shiva — the foundational story of the 51 Shakti Peethas. The Sati Kund, where she's said to have sat down in the flames, is in the temple courtyard. Far older and quieter than the Har Ki Pauri scrum, this is where the original mythology actually anchors.
why_hidden: Day-tripper itineraries hit Har Ki Pauri Ganga aarti and the Mansa Devi ropeway; Kankhal is 4km off the main drag and doesn't appear on most package tours.
best_time: Year-round; Oct-Mar most pleasant. Maha Shivratri (Feb-Mar) draws local crowds. Avoid Kanwar Mela (Jul-Aug) for chaos.
how_to_reach: 4km south of Haridwar in Kankhal. Auto-rickshaw or e-rickshaw from Haridwar railway station ~Rs 80-150.
tips: Free entry. Modest dress, bare feet inside the inner sanctum. The Sati Kund is the visual anchor — locals leave offerings there. Combine with the nearby Anandmayi Ma ashram, also in Kankhal. Best between morning and evening aartis to avoid the press of the riverfront.

name: Bhavishya Badri
description: A small Vishnu temple at Subain village 17km east of Joshimath toward Tapovan. The local prophecy — credited to a Sanat Kumar text — says when the arm of the Narsingh idol in Joshimath finally breaks, the route to Badrinath will become impassable, and the deity here will become the new Badri. The temple's stone idol is said to be slowly emerging from the rock face year by year.
why_hidden: Joshimath has been geologically unstable since 2023, and Bhavishya Badri sits in an even quieter offshoot beyond Tapovan. No tour buses run; you need a private vehicle.
best_time: May-Jun and Sep-Nov. Closed Dec-Apr by snow. Check road status post-2023 subsidence — some Joshimath access points remain affected.
how_to_reach: 17km east of Joshimath via Tapovan toward Lata. Last 2-3km is steep and rough; 4WD or local taxi recommended (Rs 2000-3000 round trip from Joshimath).
tips: No fee. Modest dress. Carry water and snacks — no shops at the temple. The road past Tapovan can close on short notice for slides; check at the Joshimath BRO/police post that morning. Combine with a Tapovan hot spring stop on the way back.

name: Kodia (Kaudia) Forest Trek
description: A dense pine and oak forest stretching toward Chamba from Kanatal — known locally as Kaudia or Kodia jungle. The marked 7-8km trail toward Chamba ridge crosses streams and a couple of meadows, with leopard pugmarks regularly seen on the soft mud after rain (you won't see the leopard). Birding here is quietly one of the best in Tehri Garhwal: cheer pheasants, koklass, and yellow-billed blue magpies.
why_hidden: Kanatal markets itself on resort packages and Tehri Lake day-trips; the Kodia trail starts behind the main road with no formal trailhead signage.
best_time: Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov. Avoid heavy monsoon (Jul-Aug) for leeches and trail erosion. Winter (Dec-Feb) gets snow, beautiful but slippery.
how_to_reach: Trailheads at the Kanatal-Chamba road junction or behind the Kanatal market. 7-8km trek to Chamba (3-4 hours one-way) or shorter loops back to Kanatal.
tips: Hire a local guide (~Rs 800-1200) for the full Chamba trek — it's not signposted. Solo walkers should stick to the shorter loops. Trekking shoes, leech socks in monsoon, layered clothes for changing weather. No food or water on the trail — pack everything.

name: Anasakti Ashram (Gandhi Ashram)
description: A small ashram on the ridge above Kausani town where Gandhi spent 14 days in June 1929 and wrote his commentary on the Bhagavad Gita's chapter on detachment — 'Anasakti Yoga'. He famously called this view 'the Switzerland of India'. The room he stayed in is preserved with his charkha and original letters; the library still operates.
why_hidden: Kausani is a 4-hour halt for most Kumaon circuits and visitors hit the tea garden viewpoint and leave; the ashram is a quiet 1km walk up from the bus stand.
best_time: Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov. Closed Tuesdays and on some festivals. Aim for early morning when the Trishul-Nanda Devi line is sharpest.
how_to_reach: Walking distance from the Kausani bus stand — 1km uphill. Open roughly 5am-12pm and 2pm-7pm. Free entry.
tips: Silence inside the prayer hall. No flash photography in Gandhi's room. The library has English-language texts on Gandhian thought; you can sit and read. The view of the 350km Himalayan stretch is the same one Gandhi praised — clearest at dawn before mist rises.

name: Sisters Bazaar
description: A short row of shops in upper Landour named for the British Army nurses who staffed the convalescent home here in the 1830s. The current cluster around Prakash's Stores and A. Prakash & Co. dates from 1928. They still sell handmade peanut butter, lemon marmalade, cured cheese, and walnut-fudge in jars labelled by hand. Ruskin Bond shops here on his rounds; ask at the bookshop next door.
why_hidden: Landour day-tourists do Char Dukan and turn back; Sisters is another 1.5km uphill on a quiet road most don't know exists.
best_time: Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov. Some shops shut Tuesdays. Open roughly 9am-6pm; closed on heavy snow days in Jan-Feb.
how_to_reach: From Landour clock tower / Char Dukan, walk 1.5km uphill on the Sisters Bazaar road. Cars allowed but parking is tight.
tips: Carry cash — UPI is patchy and the older shopkeepers prefer paper. Their peanut butter and rosehip jam are the items to actually buy. Combine with Lal Tibba viewpoint (another 1km up). Tea at the bakery counter while you decide.

name: Chauli Ki Jali Cliff
description: A natural rock outcrop 250m behind the Mukteshwar Mahadev temple — 'chauli' means rock, 'jali' means hole, and the cliff face has natural perforations local tradition reads as marks left during a battle between a goddess and a demon. The drop is sheer ~1,000m to the valley below; the IMA and local outfits use it for rock climbing and rappelling courses. The 360-degree Kumaon line from the cliff edge is the same one that put Mukteshwar on the colonial map.
why_hidden: Mukteshwar's main draws are the temple and PCRI institute; Chauli is a 5-min walk past the temple but most visitors stop at the gate and turn back.
best_time: Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov. Avoid Jul-Aug (slippery rock, no views). Winter clear days are spectacular; sunset is the sharper light.
how_to_reach: Walk 250m past the Mukteshwar temple — there's a marked stone path. Free entry. About 5 mins on foot from the temple gate.
tips: Sturdy shoes — the rock is polished smooth. No railings at the edge; keep children on hand. Rappelling/climbing operators run from the temple gate (~Rs 500-1500 per session). Avoid in heavy wind.

name: Khaliya Top
description: A high-altitude meadow at 3,600m above Munsiyari, with a clean line of sight onto the five Panchachuli peaks — the snow shelf that resembles five cooking-fires from the Pandavas' last journey. From the meadow you can see Nanda Devi and Hardeol on a clear morning. Doable as a strenuous one-day trek from Balati Farm or as a 2-day camp; in winter (Dec-Feb) the meadow is under snow and used for snow trekking.
why_hidden: Munsiyari sees a trickle of trekkers heading for Milam or Ralam glaciers; Khaliya is the day-hike option but the trailhead is a 30-min drive from Munsiyari town with no public transport.
best_time: Apr-Jun for meadows in bloom; Sep-Nov for crisp mountain views; Dec-Feb for snow trek (technical, with guide). Avoid Jul-Aug for rain.
how_to_reach: Drive 12km from Munsiyari to Balati Farm trailhead. 6km uphill trek (3-4 hours up, 2-3 down) to the meadow. Well-marked path through oak and rhododendron forest then alpine meadow.
tips: Strong fitness needed — 1,400m of elevation gain in one go. Carry 2L of water minimum; one stream halfway up. Trekking shoes mandatory. KMVN or local Munsiyari guides (~Rs 1500-2500/day) for solo travellers. Do not attempt in fresh snow without a guide.

name: Kapileshwar Mahadev Cave Temple
description: A Shiva shrine inside a natural cave on a ridge above Pithoragarh, named for the sage Kapil Muni who is said to have meditated here. The shivling sits 10m inside a dark cave reachable by a short uphill walk. The ridge above the cave gives the cleanest view of the entire Soar Valley below and the Panchachuli line on the horizon — same view as the Pithoragarh fort but without the entry queue.
why_hidden: Pithoragarh visitors do the fort, Chandak hill and Mostamanu; Kapileshwar is a 3km drive plus 15-min walk and doesn't make most district tourism brochures.
best_time: Year-round; cave is climate-stable. Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov for clearest valley views. Mahashivratri sees a small local crowd.
how_to_reach: 3km from Pithoragarh town toward Soar valley; ask for 'Kapileshwar Mahadev'. Last 500m on foot up a stone stairway.
tips: Free entry. Carry a torch — the cave entry is genuinely dark. Bare feet inside the cave; floor is damp. Combine with the Pithoragarh fort (5km from here) for a half-day local-history loop.

name: Jhula Devi Temple of Bells
description: A 700-year-old Durga temple near Chaubatia, 7km from Ranikhet, walled and roofed with thousands of brass bells donated by devotees whose prayers were answered. The clanging carries across the valley on a still afternoon. The bells are tied to every available beam and railing; some date back over a century. The current shrine structure is from 1935.
why_hidden: Ranikhet's standard tourist circuit is golf course and Chaubatia gardens; Jhula Devi is 1km off the Chaubatia road, easy to miss.
best_time: Year-round. Mar-Jun and Sep-Nov pleasant. Navratri (twice a year) sees crowds; off-festival mornings are quietest.
how_to_reach: 7km from Ranikhet bus stand on the Chaubatia road. Local bus or taxi; the temple has a small parking area. Open roughly 6am-7pm.
tips: Free entry. Buy a small bell from the shops outside (Rs 50-300) to hang yourself if your prayer is answered. Combine with Chaubatia gardens (1km away) and the orchard tasting room. Modest dress; remove leather goods at the gate.

name: Koteshwar Dam Reservoir
description: The lower companion to the famous Tehri Dam — a 97.5m run-of-the-river structure on the Bhagirathi, 22km downstream from Tehri Lake. The reservoir behind it is narrower and quieter than Tehri Lake, with rope-bridges and small ghats from the older villages still visible at the waterline. The Koteshwar Mahadev temple, after which the dam is named, sits on the bank and is the original anchor of the place — the dam came later.
why_hidden: Tehri Lake gets all the visitor traffic; Koteshwar is the second dam in the same hydro complex and most road-trippers don't realise it's there.
best_time: Year-round. Sep-Nov for clearest water and post-monsoon greenery. Avoid heavy monsoon for landslides on the access road.
how_to_reach: 22km downstream of Tehri Dam, near Pratapnagar. Drive from New Tehri ~45 mins. The Koteshwar Mahadev temple is on the reservoir's east bank.
tips: No entry fee at the dam viewpoint, but no public access onto the dam itself (security). Photography of the powerhouse restricted. Combine with the Koteshwar Mahadev temple (free) and a meal at the Pratapnagar bazaar. Carry ID — random checks on the access road.

name: Dayara Bugyal
description: A 28 sq km high-altitude meadow at 3,000-3,500m above Barsu/Raithal villages, 32km from Uttarkashi. In winter it's one of the few accessible snow-trek meadows in Garhwal; in summer it's wildflower-thick — primulas, asters, brahma kamal in late August. The peaks visible include Bandarpunch, Black Peak (Kalanag) and Srikanth — the same sweep that Sankri/Har Ki Dun trekkers travel further to see.
why_hidden: Uttarkashi visitors are mostly Char Dham yatris en route to Gangotri; Dayara is 32km off the Gangotri road via Bhatwari.
best_time: Apr-Jun (greens), Aug-Sep (flowers — late monsoon), Oct-Nov (clear skies), Dec-Feb (snow trek with operator). Avoid heavy monsoon Jul.
how_to_reach: Drive 32km from Uttarkashi to Raithal village (1.5 hours). 7km uphill trek from Raithal (4-5 hours one-way) or 5km from Barsu. Camp permitted.
tips: Easy-to-moderate trek; OK for first-timers with reasonable fitness. KMVN huts at Dayara top. Carry warm layers — the meadow gets cold even in summer. NIM Uttarkashi or local guides (~Rs 1500-2500/day). Don't camp inside the meadow proper — use the designated edges to protect the grass.
